title: Challenges and Opportunities of Moderating Usage of Large Language Models in Education
extended_summary:
This paper examines how large language models, specifically ChatGPT, can be moderated for educational use to reduce overreliance and encourage students’ reflection and critical thinking. The authors focus on a known concern in education: when students have unrestricted access to LLMs, they may copy answers without engaging deeply with the task. The study asks whether modifying how ChatGPT responds can improve students’ interaction strategies and support better learning-related behaviors while solving physics problems.

To investigate this, the authors developed two moderated ChatGPT-based tools: a Multi-Response Bot that provides three different candidate answers, and a Hint Bot that provides hints instead of direct solutions. These were compared against two baseline conditions: unrestricted ChatGPT access via a Classic Bot and an internet Search Engine. In a between-subject online experiment, 40 students were randomly assigned to one of the four conditions and completed a pretest plus two challenging free-response physics problems. The researchers analyzed both objective performance scores and qualitative interaction logs, coding behaviors such as copy-paste use, reflection, preprocessing/priming strategies, and use of the tools as substitutes for calculators or translators.

Participants were students with prior physics knowledge, many studying physics or other STEM fields, and the study appears to have been conducted in Germany through institutions including DFKI, RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau, and LMU Munich. The study took place fully online on researcher-hosted websites. Students had approximately 30 minutes total, including an 8-item pretest, tutorials for the assigned tool, and two timed physics questions. Performance was scored by physics experts, while usability and perceived correctness/quality of the tools were also collected.

The main findings were that moderated LLM use changed interaction behavior in desirable ways, especially by reducing unreflected copy-and-paste usage compared with unmoderated ChatGPT. The Multi-Response Bot produced reflection rates and performance closest to the search engine condition, while the Hint Bot led to more attempts to manipulate the tool and lower performance. However, no statistically significant differences in final performance were found across conditions, and chatbot usability was significantly worse than the search engine. The authors conclude that moderation of LLM outputs is a promising direction for educational AI design, but that effectiveness depends heavily on interface design, usability, and alignment with student expectations.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's large language model chatbot used for conversational question answering and assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Students used ChatGPT-based tools to answer two free-response physics problems. The paper studied unmoderated ChatGPT access ('Classic Bot') and two moderated ChatGPT variants: a Multi-Response Bot that returned three alternative answers and a Hint Bot that provided hints instead of direct solutions.

findings.finding_summary: In a between-subject study with N=40 students, performance on two physics free-text questions differed descriptively by condition but not significantly after aligned-rank-transform ANOVA. Mean main-test scores were Search Engine 2.5 (SD=1.38, n=12), Multi-Response Bot 2.3 (SD=2.21, n=10), Classic Bot 1.62 (SD=1.77, n=8), and Hint Bot 1.1 (SD=0.57, n=10), indicating moderated ChatGPT could approach search-engine performance descriptively while unmoderated ChatGPT and hint-only support performed worse.
findings.measure: Physics main-test score on two free-text questions scored by raters (0-8 points, with theoretical bonus on question 2)

findings.finding_summary: Moderated ChatGPT conditions showed less non-reflective use than unmoderated ChatGPT. Non-reflection strategies accounted for 21.2% of Multi-Response Bot queries and 22.7% of Hint Bot queries versus 46.7% for Classic Bot; reflection strategies were 50.0% for Multi-Response Bot and 38.6% for Hint Bot versus 33.3% for Classic Bot, although internet search still had the highest reflection share at 57.5%.
findings.measure: Coded interaction strategies from prompts/query logs: non-reflection, preprocessing, reflection, tool substitute

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT-based interfaces had lower usability than the search-engine baseline, and waiting times were longer for moderated bots. SUS/UMUX-Lite-derived usability means were 47.3 (SD=17.4) for Multi-Response Bot, 55.4 (SD=12.5) for Hint Bot, and 48.0 (SD=18.8) for Classic Bot versus 73.0 (SD=13.1) for Search Engine; a one-way ANOVA found a significant main effect, F(3,36)=6.7, p<0.01, with significant pairwise differences between Search Engine and Multi-Response Bot and between Search Engine and Classic Bot.
findings.measure: Usability (UMUX-Lite converted to SUS), response/wait time

findings.finding_summary: Participants rated ChatGPT-based outputs as less correct than search results in some cases. Correctness ratings showed a significant main effect of tool type, F(3,36)=3.8, p<0.05; Search Engine was rated 77.2 (SD=16.5) versus 48.6 (SD=21.3) for Multi-Response Bot, with a significant pairwise difference, while no significant differences were found for answer-quality ratings.
findings.measure: Participant ratings of tool answer correctness and quality on 0-100 scales

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical between-subject user study with random assignment and reported sample sizes, but it is small (N=40) and does not report strong causal effect estimates or significant learning gains between conditions. The evidence is stronger than opinion work but below rigorous large-scale RCT/QED standards.
impact_tier_rationale: Findings suggest potentially beneficial changes in reflective behavior from moderated ChatGPT use, but academic performance differences were not statistically significant and usability drawbacks were substantial. Overall impact is mixed and unclear rather than clearly positive.
